source.name: NASA/NSSDCA planetary fact sheets
note: 302-redirects to https://www.nasa.gov/nssdc/ as of 2026-09-09, so the
dated Wayback snapshot is the citation. Per-row `factSheetLabel` names
which published quantity the value is, because for the giant planets the
fact sheets publish more than one and the choice changes the answer.

dropComparison.reason: The vacuum panel's anchor: Apollo 15, David Scott, 2 August 1971, hammer and falcon feather landing together on film.
Clearly quicker than the Moon and clearly slower than Earth, so the middle rung is visible without measurement.
The child's own reference point, and the only panel where the air panel and the airless panel differ.

dropComparison.factSheetLabel: Surface gravity (mean) at the 1 bar level, m/s2
dropComparison.equatorialFactSheetLabel: Surface gravity (eq.) at the 1 bar level, m/s2
dropComparison.reason: Stronger than Earth under BOTH published columns (25.92 and 23.12 against 9.82), so the claim does not depend on which one is read. This is the test Saturn fails. Jupiter has no surface either, but nothing here says the stone lands.

excluded.factSheetLabel: Surface gravity (mean) at the 1 bar level, m/s2
excluded.equatorialFactSheetLabel: Surface gravity (eq.) at the 1 bar level, m/s2
excluded.reason: NOT ATTESTED for this beat. The two published columns straddle Earth in opposite directions: 11.19 m/s2 is 1.14x Earth, 8.96 m/s2 is 0.92x Earth. Whether a stone falls faster or slower than at home would be decided by which column an author picked, not by Saturn. Do not add it back.
Recorded, but never to be shown beside Mars: 3.70 against 3.73 is the same number at published precision. Asking a child to see that difference teaches that invisible differences are visible.
Almost exactly Earth's, so a side-by-side drop shows nothing. Recorded so the row is never re-typed from memory if a later level wants it.
Off the scale of any drawable drop, and there is no surface to stand on. Recorded only so the number is never invented.
